claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by atomic-ordering kinetics driven by preferential Al partitioning.
Slow cooling or extended thermal exposure triggers transformation of the high-temperature BCC state into an ordered intermetallic phase such as B2.
Sufficient cooling time or aging permits Al, and possibly Ni, to partition and order.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and ordering.
Local chemical inhomogeneity, particularly Al segregation, facilitates nucleation of an ordered intermetallic phase within the matrix.
During slow cooling or thermal exposure, increased atomic mobility causes Al to partition and become locally concentrated.
Local Al enrichment drives an order-disorder transformation in which part of the BCC matrix reorganizes into an ordered intermetallic phase.
Rapid quenching freezes the disordered atomic configuration and preserves the high-temperature BCC phase.
Slow-cooled or thermally aged samples will exhibit additional diffraction peaks indicating an ordered phase.
Slow-cooled or thermally aged samples will contain nanometer-scale precipitates detectable by TEM.
Rapidly quenched samples will largely retain a homogeneous BCC structure without ordered-phase diffraction or microstructural features.
DSC should reveal thermal events associated with an order-disorder transition.
The proposed mechanism should cease to operate at cooling rates or temperatures for which diffusion is negligible.
